hypothesis: If Darwin is right, no island lying more than 300 statute miles (482.8 km) from a continent or from a great continental island has a native non-volant terrestrial mammal; every non-flying land mammal found on such islands is a human introduction.
pass_criterion: Among pre-registered island units whose representative point lies > 482.8 km from the nearest landmass of area >= 100,000 km2 (continents and great islands, computed from Natural Earth 1:50m land polygons), zero units have a non-volant, non-marine mammal species endemic to the unit by GBIF occurrence data (>= 10 non-fossil, non-captive records worldwide, >= 95 % inside the unit). Endemism is used as conservative proof of native status; bats (Chiroptera), cetaceans, sirenians, pinnipeds and Homo sapiens are excluded.
fail_criterion: At least one far unit has >= 2 endemic non-volant terrestrial mammal species, or >= 2 far units each have >= 1: refutes (more than 'a single instance' and not attributable to one doubtful record). Exactly one far unit with exactly one endemic species: mixed. The share of far units with native terrestrial mammals is reported either way.
interpretation: Darwin's 'terrestrial mammal' is read as a non-volant, non-marine mammal (he treats bats separately in the next sentence and excludes domesticated animals). 'Continent or great continental island' is operationalised as any landmass polygon of area >= 100,000 km2, which captures the continents plus Greenland, New Guinea, Borneo, Madagascar, Sumatra, Honshu, Britain, Sulawesi, Java, Luzon, New Zealand's islands, Newfoundland, Cuba and Iceland; including a few non-continental large islands can only shorten distances and so makes the test conservative. Distance is the great-circle distance from a representative point of the island unit to the nearest vertex of those polygons (segments densified), excluding the polygon containing the point itself.
